title: Hyperbolic crochet
hook: A shape mathematicians found hard to model was finally made with a crochet hook.
peek: Hyperbolic space curves away from itself at every point, like a lettuce leaf. In 1997 the mathematician Daina Taimina found the best way to hold it in your hands: crochet it, adding stitches at a steady rate until it ruffles.
lede: Hyperbolic geometry, worked out in the 1800s, describes surfaces where space keeps opening up, so parallel lines spread apart and triangles have thin, inward-curving sides. It is hard to picture and hard to build. Paper models fell apart easily. In 1997 Daina Taimina, a Latvian mathematician at Cornell, realised that crochet could do it, producing ruffled, coral-like shapes.

bullets.text: The method is simple: crochet a row, then add an extra stitch every few stitches, again and again. Each row has more stitches than the last by a fixed proportion, so the fabric grows exponentially and has to ruffle to fit.

The geometer William Thurston had built hyperbolic surfaces by taping together paper rings. They worked but were fragile. Taimina's crocheted versions could be folded, stretched and thrown in a bag without losing their shape.
Taimina wrote a book about the method, published in 2009. It won the Diagram Prize for the year's oddest book title, though it is a serious guide to the geometry.

Inspired by Taimina, the sisters Margaret and Christine Wertheim began a crocheted coral reef in 2005. Thousands of people have since added pieces, and the reefs have been shown in museums around the world.
